A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CRAG and share the same core method and benchmark results. Both are readable throughout: v1 ends after its references, while v2 includes Appendices A–C. Text, figures, tables and equations support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original assembly experiments on PartNeXt and Breaking Bad in Table 1, component ablations in Table 2, and qualitative reconstruction and failure results in Figures 3–7.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds completion comparisons, generation-quality measurements, fragment-count analyses and additional qualitative examples in Tables 2, 3 and 5 and Figure 8.

M1.justification: The shared VAE, coupled assembly/generation branches, bidirectional adapters, flow objectives and two-stage training remain unchanged. Appendix A newly documents details such as QK normalization, per-part pose tokens and timestep sampling; the PDFs do not establish that these replace different choices used in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use PartNeXt, Breaking Bad, MorphoSource and FRACTURA, covering assembly, generation, missing parts and optional reference images. The new generation measurements, fragment-count breakdown and anatomical statistics concern existing coverage rather than establishing a new dataset, population or task.

E2.justification: v2 adds SDFusion and MGPC as evaluated shape-completion baselines in Table 2, substantially extending comparison beyond assembly methods. It also quantifies the previously qualitative TripoSG comparison in Table 3. GARF, RPF and Assembler remain in the original assembly comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include ground-truth alignment for completion baselines, randomly selected reference views for generation evaluation on 4,626 shapes, CD-L1/CD-L2, F-scores, EMD, decoding-failure measurement and PA stratification by fragment count. The original assembly settings remain unchanged; the relationship between the new 4,626-shape evaluation and Section 4.2's retained 3,903-shape evaluation is unexplained.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic fragment-count robustness results in Table 5 and decoding-failure analysis in Table 3. Appendix A.4 reports qualitative findings from testing concatenated joint attention against bidirectional cross-attention, and Figure 8 adds reconstruction cases. The original component ablations and failure examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added decoding-failure frequencies are outcome measurements, without accompanying uncertainty estimates or a changed statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original ablation scores remain unchanged. New results include completion CD-L1 values of 22.51 for SDFusion, 12.59 for MGPC and 9.39 for CRAG, in the displayed ×10−2 units; 25.0% decoding failures for TripoSG versus 0% for CRAG; and PA advantages over Assembler of 11.4 points at two parts and 22.8 at ten parts. These are newly reported comparisons, not performance improvements over v1 under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds Equations 9–14 defining vertex projections, extremal thresholds and force-application regions for fracture simulation. This is a limited addition of mathematical specification. The core flow-matching equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about mutually beneficial assembly and generation, missing-part robustness, state-of-the-art assembly and the curated bone dataset. The added experiments support these existing claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new completion comparison as supporting joint over sequential reasoning and the fragment-count results as showing increasing value from holistic priors. Appendix A adds explanations for preprocessing and training choices. Existing failure mechanisms, applicability limitations and future-work discussion remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B substantially expand implementation documentation with point counts, normalization, PCA alignment, augmentation, FPS, network dimensions and parameter counts, pose tokens, optimizer scheduling, precision and fracture-loading procedures. These are primarily newly disclosed details. The original training budgets, hardware information and promise to release code and models remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for SDFusion, MGPC, Marching Cubes and PCA, and explicitly compares CRAG with sequential assembly-then-completion approaches. Section 2 and the broader positioning relative to assembly and generative-model research remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include a localized rewrite of the generation-evaluation discussion, added experimental subheadings and structured Appendices A–C, plus conference and acknowledgment formatting. The original narrative is not extensively reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds five tables covering completion, generation, fragment counts, dataset composition and architecture, plus Figure 8 with three new qualitative cases. The original ablation table becomes Table 4, and Figures 5–7 are repositioned. These additions substantially expand the visual and tabular presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 supported the generation side of its central contribution mainly through qualitative examples. v2 adds quantitative generation evidence, tests the important sequential-completion alternative and supplies substantial implementation and simulation details, addressing central validation and reproducibility gaps. The unexplained evaluation-set sizes and unspecified handling of failed meshes in aggregate quality metrics limit interpretation, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.
